"All emergency services are performing exceptionally in the toughest conditions, to fight the flames, protect people, and limit damages. As well as firefighters, state police and the military, the federal police is in operation with its airborne units and the THW [Germany's federal civil protection agency, made up largely of volunteers, that assists in emergency situations] is helping with logistics and operational coordination," Dobrindt said. Dobrindt's ministry had similarly listed the efforts by various services in a social media post earlier on Friday. It also noted that there were "several localized vegetation fires" dotted around the country in various states — North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland and Saxony — on Friday, but said that, with the exception of Hürtgenwald, they were "for the most part under control and have been almost completely extinguished by regional responders." https://p.dw.com/p/5IrRp Skip next section 5 injured amid fire: 4 rescue workers and 1 elderly resident 08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 5 injured amid fire: 4 rescue workers and 1 elderly resident Four of the responders on scene sustained mild injuries during their work, a local politician reported Image: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance Local politician Christian Nolten has told the dpa news agency that five people have suffered injuries amid Friday's evacuation and firefighting efforts. One elderly man suffered a heart complaint during the operations to clear the village of Gey, Nolten said. And four rescue workers sustained light injuries, such as cuts and circulatory problems, amid their work. The public gathering point for those affected has been moved further away from the site of the fire, to a special needs school in Düren, for people's safety. Two initial gathering points closer to the fire have since been closed because of a buildup of smoke and ash in the area. The next village of Grosshau, to the south of Gey and the heart of the fire, has not yet been evacuated. "The Gey settlement has been evacuated. And for safety reasons, we will not allow residents to return tonight," Thielen told the KSTA. He said that the situation remained fluid, to such an extent that rescue teams were having to reposition their own facilities. "We've just had to dismantle our staging area because it, too, is at risk because of the changing weather conditions," he said. "This means we're reorganizing, redeploying our personnel and planning our next steps." Thielen said that authorities had already planned for personnel deployments on a rough basis through to Monday morning, "and then we may need to reassess the situation and potentially request additional personnel." Even with the surrounding area closed off, traffic jams formed at times on Friday as various rescue services and other vehicles headed to the scene Image: Volker Danisch/dpa/picture alliance https://p.dw.com/p/5IrOr Skip next section What was the Battle of Hürtgen Forest, the reason WWII ordnances are strewn about the area? 08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 What was the Battle of Hürtgen Forest, the reason WWII ordnances are strewn about the area? Tens of thousands of troops on both sides were killed or wounded in the Battle of Hürtgen Forest in World War II Image: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance Friday's fire is taking place on the site of one of the longest and most costly single battles in the US military's history. That's why the area is strewn with unexploded munitions from World War II that are at risk of exploding, both aiding the fire's spread and potentially endangering emergency services. The Battle of Hürtgen Forest, or Schlacht im Hürtgenwald in German, was a three-month push by US forces. They were trying at first to pin down German forces and stop them providing reinforcements in the nearby Battle of Aachen, and then later to push through the forest and advance to the Rur River. The September-December 1944 battle tried to get through heavy fortifications as part of what the Allies knew as the Siegfried Line, a series of defensive structures that served as one of Nazi Germany's last effective lines of defense as Allied forces tried to move east toward Berlin after the D-Day landings. Some ruined tanks are preserved as they were left stricken within the forest as monuments Image: ABBfoto/picture alliance Germany's military was already planning its Winter Offensive, which would be known as the Battle of the Bulge, in the same area by this point, and so its troops were given all possible resources for their defensive efforts. The battle was seen as a comparatively rare Nazi victory in their attempts to stop the Allied advance, with at least 33,000 US casualties, and some estimates ranging considerably higher than that. Germany, with more strains on personnel and supply but also with the defenders' advantage and favorable terrain, suffered an estimated 28,000 casualties. It's less well remembered than the much larger and more widespread Battle of the Bulge , whose main thrust was located slightly further south but in the same Eifel region. Nevertheless, it was the longest continuous battle on German ground during World War II and the second-longest single battle the US Army has ever fought. There's a war memorial, cemetery and peace museum in Vossenack in the Düren municipality — several kilometers south of the site of the fire Image: Daniela Natalie Posdnjakov/DW https://p.dw.com/p/5IrGO Skip next section Cologne police launch appeal for information on fire's outbreak 08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Cologne police launch appeal for information on fire's outbreak Police in the city of Cologne are investigating the cause of the Hürtgenwald fire and are appealing for help from members of the public who might be able to shed light on how it started. Police said in a press statement and public appeal that they had set up an online web portal where people could upload information in an "uncomplicated and direct" manner, straight to law enforcement. "The Cologne Police asks the public for support in the ongoing investigations. Of particular interest are clues and particularly picture or video recordings from the rough time of the start of the fire," police wrote. "Such recordings could deliver important findings and help the investigative work meaningfully." The appeal provided a link to the site where uploads are possible, and police wrote that "any clue could be meaningful" as they seek to establish the cause of the fire. Almost all forest fires are ultimately man-made — whether they're caused by accident or oversight or as a more deliberate act of arson. Even in the driest and hottest summer temperatures, the heat required to trigger a fire among trees is almost never achieved by natural means — with the only plausible all-natural scenario being a lightning strike. The high summer temperatures and dry forest floor, rather than starting the fires, provide conditions suitable to enable and accelerate the spread after it's begun. https://p.dw.com/p/5IrAl Skip next section State premier Hendrik Wüst breaking off holiday to return 08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 State premier Hendrik Wüst breaking off holiday to return The head of North Rhine-Westphalia's state government is breaking off his vacation to return amid the fire. She said the government in Germany's most populous state is now working on the assumption that this was the largest forest fire in the state, at least in decades if not on record. "We at least are not aware of a forest fire that reached this size," Gorissen said. "It could well be that it really is the biggest since our state was founded, and that shows what we're dealing with here." She said she was working on the assumption that at least 200 hectares were affected but acknowledged that higher estimates were in play, saying "perhaps we're even knocking on the door of 300." Gorissen told the dpa news agency that she could already see the smoke as she was approaching the scene. "It really is a bit apocalyptic," she said. "It's a very imposing sight, a sad sight, seeing the forests in flame," she said. She praised the emergency responders and the speed with which such a large multi-force response was put together. section Fire service: 'Under no circumstances' are residents likely to return this evening 08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Fire service: 'Under no circumstances' are residents likely to return this evening Tanks and other equipment is being used to try to carve out a containment line in a perimeter around the fire, stopping its spread Image: Federico Gambarini/dpa/picture alliance A firefighters' spokesman, Peter Berndgen, has told the dpa news agency that he does not expect locals in Gey to be able to return to their homes on Friday. By his estimation, Berndgen said, "under no circumstances" was this likely. Local politician Ralf Nolten similarly suggested the evacuation could continue, saying "we need to be able to work freely," with clear roads to allow vehicles easy access to the area. Berndgen said the efforts to extinguish the blaze could take days. "We have very unfortunate conditions for fighting a forest fire today," he said, calling it a "red flag day" — with high temperatures, high humidity and high winds all fanning the flames. Berndgen said specialist teams were using machine saws, tanks and other equipment to try to rapidly cut trees and form a 15-meter (49-foot) containment line around the fire, seeking to deny it the fuel it needs to spread. https://p.dw.com/p/5IqXB Skip next section Where is the Hürtgenwald region of Germany? 08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Where is the Hürtgenwald region of Germany? https://p.dw.com/p/5IqDX Skip next section Merz thanks emergency services fighting Eifel wildfires 08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Merz thanks emergency services fighting Eifel wildfires Chancellor Friedrich Merz has voiced thanks to emergency services fighting the wildfires near the Dutch and Belgian borders. https://www.cambstimes.co.uk/news/nation.text: Polish school attacks driven by ‘glorification of violence’ online, says Tusk By PA News Agency Share 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. The attacks at Polish schools over the past week were “spontaneous acts” driven by the online “glorification of violence”, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said. Three attacks at schools in Mazovian province in central Poland took place within four days, leaving one dead and many injured, including children. By Sunday morning, police had detained 117 people across Poland for carrying knives or other dangerous weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students. Some 64,000 schools were checked. “We are not dealing with any group organised on a big scale,” Mr Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with government and security services. “These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity. “In the past years and months, we have noted – globally and in Poland – a rise in the fascination with violence.” Three attacks have taken place at schools in Poland this week (Claudia Ciobanu/AP) Mr Tusk said the acts could be associated with “nihilistic violence”, a term used by authorities to describe acts of violence driven by a nihilistic worldview and misanthropy rather than specific political goals. In the case of Poland, he said “some of the people detained are active in the ultra-right environment”. He said authorities have observed intensified online searches of Nazi content as well as of “mass killers who have become idols online”. Mr Tusk said Poland is facing a “civilisational phenomenon” where children are playing video games, even banal ones, or becoming interested in crime stories and are then getting exposed to more and more violence. Kacper Rekawek, senior researcher at the International Centre for Counterterrorism in The Hague, said: “This is essentially a copycat scenario, something of a long trail of attackers going back to at least 2019, if not decades earlier.” He was referring to Brenton Tarrant, the white supremacist who shot and killed 51 Muslims at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 2019. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said police checks will continue at Polish schools (PA) Mr Rekawek said one of the suspects in the latest Polish attacks used the same imagery and aesthetics as Tarrant, which means the Polish incidents should be “placed within the confines of essentially terrorist behaviour”. Mr Tusk said police checks at schools across Poland would continue into next week in case children exposed to the stories of the past attacks might “get stupid and unsafe thoughts” to imitate them. He said Poland has lots of work to do as a society, with parents and teachers having an especially important role to play in communicating with children about their experiences online and explaining that “fascination and membership in these online practices can lead to very negative consequences”. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in Mazovian province attacked fellow students, teachers and passers-by with a sharp object, wounding nine people. He was arrested nearby. The following day, a 15-year-old killed a school custodian and wounded two other people in a knife attack at his former school in the same province. On Saturday, a 21-year old woman wounded three at a post-secondary school in Warsaw. Rumours that the attacks were co-ordinated and that there would be more on “bloody Friday” were shared in parents’ online groups and by mainstream media. It led to 59 schools pre-emptively suspending classes on Friday across Poland, the majority in Mazovian province. Those detained on Friday by the police include a 14-year-old boy from Warsaw who was found in possession of a knife with a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers, and a 16-year-old who came to school with a butterfly knife in his backpack, police said. Meanwhile, Poland’s interior minister said on Sunday that a man who threatened and planned to attack Mr Tusk has been arrested. Marcin Kierwinski gave no details about the identity of the man nor the type of attack that was allegedly planned. “The man who threatened an attack was detained,” Mr Tusk wrote on X. “Thanks to the police for fast and decisive action.” A government spokesperson told Polish media that Mr Tusk learned about the threat first thing on Sunday morning. He said that, even if officials do occasionally get threats, this one was “exceptionally concerning”. Share Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading...
